title: Given two sorted arrays, find the median of the combined sorted order of all elements in O(log(min(m, n))) time, without actually merging the arrays.
shortTitle: Median of Two Sorted Arrays: Binary Search Partition
keyPoints: Binary-search a partition in the smaller array; derive the complementary partition in the larger array.
The partition is correct when every element on the left side is less than or equal to every element on the right side.
For odd totals, the median is the max of the two left-side values; for even totals, it is the average of the left max and right min.
Always search the shorter array to bound time at O(log(min(m, n))) and keep the derived partition in bounds.
Use negative and positive infinity as sentinels at the edges to handle empty partitions without special branches.
The brute-force merge approach is O(m + n) and simpler, but the binary search approach is the optimal answer.

s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search a partition of the smaller array so the two combined halves are balanced; read the median at the boundary.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Partition approach** – draw a virtual cut through both arrays so the left combined half and right combined half have equal counts.
- **Binary search** – search the cut position in the smaller array; derive the cut in the larger array from the half-length formula.
- **Balance condition** – the partition is correct when left-max of A <= right-min of B and left-max of B <= right-min of A.
- **Sentinel values** – use negative/positive infinity at array edges to handle empty partitions cleanly.
- **Complexity** – O(log(min(m, n))) time, O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, two sorted ledgers from the savings and current-account systems must be combined to find the median transaction amount. Instead of merging both fully, a clerk draws a vertical cut through both ledgers at once so the total number of rows on the left equals the number on the right, and every value on the left is no larger than every value on the right. The median sits at the boundary.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
A = [100, 300, 500, 700]   (m=4)
B = [200, 400, 600, 800]   (n=4)
half = (4+4+1)/2 = 4

Binary search on A (shorter or equal):

low=0, high=4
  i=2, j=4-2=2
  aLeftMax=300, aRightMin=500
  bLeftMax=400, bRightMin=600
  300 <= 600 ✓  but  400 > 500 ✗ -> low = 3

low=3, high=4
  i=3, j=4-3=1
  aLeftMax=500, aRightMin=700
  bLeftMax=200, bRightMin=400
  500 > 400 ✗ -> high = 2

Wait, let me redo: low=0, high=4
  i=2, j=2: aLM=300, aRM=500, bLM=400, bRM=600
  bLM(400) > aRM(500)? No. aLM(300) > bRM(600)? No.
  Both conditions hold! Balanced.
  Even total: (max(300,400) + min(500,600)) / 2 = (400+500)/2 = 450.0
```

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│   Median of Two Sorted Arrays Flow            │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                              │
│   Ensure A is shorter (swap if needed)       │
│              │                               │
│              ▼                               │
│   Binary search: low=0, high=m               │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────┐           │
│   │ i = mid of [low, high]       │           │
│   │ j = half - i                 │           │
│   │ Check: aLM<=bRM && bLM<=aRM │           │
│   │   Yes: read median           │           │
│   │   aLM > bRM: high = i-1      │           │
│   │   bLM > aRM: low = i+1       │           │
│   └──────────────────────────────┘           │
│                                              │
│   Odd total:  max(aLM, bLM)                 │
│   Even total: avg(max(lefts), min(rights))   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the median of two sorted arrays in logarithmic time is one of the hardest binary search problems. The key idea is that you never merge the arrays. Instead, you binary-search a partition position in the shorter array and derive the complementary partition in the longer array so the left combined half and right combined half are correctly balanced.

The partition is correct when every element on the left is less than or equal to every element on the right. Once balanced, the median sits at the boundary: for an odd total, it is the larger of the two left-edge values; for an even total, it is the average of the left max and right min.

At the National Bank of India, the analytics team needed the median transaction amount across two sorted datasets from the savings and current-account systems. Merging two large datasets just to read the middle value would be wasteful, so the partition method gave the median in logarithmic time.

The details that make the code clean are sentinel values at array edges and always searching the shorter array. Sentinels handle empty partitions without branching, and searching the shorter array bounds the time and keeps the derived cut in bounds.

Remember one sentence: binary-search a partition in the shorter array so the two combined halves are balanced, and read the median at the boundary.
